rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The name al-mathānī is explained by the Fātiḥa having been revealed twice.
rows.anchor: لأنها نزلت مرتين

rows.speaker: أبى بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy reports that the Prophet called the Fātiḥa the unmatched Mother of the Qur’an and seven oft-repeated verses, divided between God and servant, with the servant receiving what he asks.
rows.anchor: وعن أبى بن كعب، قال: قرأت على رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - فاتحة الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ism derives from sumu, elevation, rather than simah, mark: its plural is asmāʾ, its diminutive sumayy, and words losing an initial radical do not take hamzat al-waṣl in this way.
rows.anchor: الأول أصح؛ لأنهم جمعوه على أسماء، وقالوا في تصغيره سمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed root of ism is elevation (also linked with samāʾ), a mark, or the verb meaning to rise and become manifest as a sign of the underlying meaning.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من السمة، والأول أصح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ism can weigh fiʿl with either ḍamma or kasra, but not faʿl with fatḥa, since its regular plural would be afʿul rather than afʿāl.
rows.anchor: يجوز فعل، وفعل بضم الفاء وكسرها، ولا يجوز فعل بفتح الفاء

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: One derivation takes Allah from ilāh, dropping the hamza and making the alif-lām an obligatory substitute so the name becomes a proper name.
rows.anchor: هذا مذهب سيبويه، وقيل: أصله لاه، ألحقت بها الألف واللام

rows.speaker: الخليل وأبي علي
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl and Abū ʿAlī regard Allah as an un-derived name; not every word must be derived, or derivation would regress without end.
rows.anchor: هذا مذهب الخليل وأبي علي. وقيل: إنه مشتق

rows.speaker: النضر بن شميل
rows.claim: A group including al-Naḍr b. Shumayl derives Allah from taʾalluh, worship; Ibn ʿAbbās read ilāhatak as your worship, and a poetic line uses taʾalluh for devotion.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس: وإلهتك، أي عبادتك، قال الشاعر: سبحن واسترجعن من تأله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other derivations connect Allah with seeking refuge in someone, bewilderment (Abū ʿAmr), finding repose with someone (al-Mubarrad), or concealment from lāha.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو مشتق من الوله، وهو التحير، يقال: أله يأله، إذا تحير عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm derive from mercy, whose basis is benefaction to the needy; both are intensive forms, with faʿlān more emphatic than faʿīl because it departs further from the base pattern.
rows.anchor: والرحمن الرحيم: اسمان مشتقان من الرحمة، وأصل الرحمة: النعمة

rows.speaker: أبي عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr explains Allah as the one whose essential greatness leaves minds bewildered.
rows.anchor: معناه: أنه تتحير العقول في كنه عظمته، كما يقال للمكتوب: كتاب، عن أبي عمرو بن العلاء

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad explains Allah as the one whose remembrance creatures find repose in.
rows.anchor: معناه: أن الخلق يسكنون إلى ذكره، عن المبرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported explanation is that God is seen but does not see.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه: أنه يرى ولا يرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gloss “the worshipped one” is wrong because others besides God are worshipped and are not gods.
rows.anchor: فأما من قال: معناه: المعبود فقد أخطأ؛ لأن غيره عبد، وليس بإله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defining Allah as “the one entitled to worship” wrongly implies that He was not God in eternity.
rows.anchor: ومن قال: إنه المستحق للعبادة يلزمه ألا يكون إلها في الأزل، وهذا خطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as synonymous names for the merciful, like nadmān and nadīm.
rows.anchor: قيل: معناهما واحد، وهو ذو الرحمة، كندمان ونديم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view distinguishes the names because other beings may be called raḥīm but not raḥmān.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بينهما فرق، ولذلك يسمى غيره رحيما، ولا يسمى رحمانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One distinction makes al-Raḥmān the provider for all creatures and al-Raḥīm the forgiver of all believers.
rows.anchor: قيل: الرحمن: الرازق لجميع خلقه، والرحيم: الغافر لجميع المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another makes al-Raḥmān the giver of foundational blessings only God can create, while al-Raḥīm denotes one possessing mercy.
rows.anchor: الرازق لجميع خلقه، والرحيم: الغافر لجميع المؤمنين، وقيل: الرحمن: فاعل أصول النعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further distinction assigns al-Raḥmān to creation and al-Raḥīm to provision.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الرحمن بالخلق، والرحيم بالرزق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pairing intensifies the attribution of mercy and teaches that all blessings come from God.
rows.anchor: للمبالغة بصفته بالرحمة؛ ليعلم أن النعم كلها منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Arabs commonly knew Allah but not al-Raḥmān, the names are paired to show that Allah, al-Raḥmān, and al-Raḥīm all name and describe Him.
rows.anchor: لأن العرب كثير في لغتهم لفظ، (الله)، ولم يعرفوا الرحمن، فجمع بينهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says al-Raḥmān is more frequent in the Torah, al-Raḥīm in the Gospel, and Allah in the Qur’an, so the pairing shows all refer to God.
rows.anchor: لأن في التوراة ذكر الرحمن أكثر، وفي الإنجيل ذكر الرحيم أكثر، وفي القرآن ذكر الله أكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm because its stronger intensity and exclusive use make it like a proper name, and the more definite name comes first.
rows.anchor: لأنه لما كان أشد مبالغة، ولا يوصف به غيره صار كالعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three names in the basmala serve seeking aid: God can bestow every blessing and has ample mercy and beneficence.
rows.anchor: لأن الغرض الاستعانة، ولكل واحد منها تأثير في ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beginning an important undertaking by naming God is recommended because it seeks His aid, acknowledges divinity, and admits His blessing; a report says an important matter begun without it is cut off.
rows.anchor: الآية تدل على أن ذكر اسم الله في ابتداء الأمر مسنون؛ لأن في ذلك استعانة به

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala is recited once, in the first rakʿa.
rows.anchor: فقيل: يقرأ مرة في الركعة الأولى، عن أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: أبو يوسف
rows.claim: Abū Yūsuf holds that the basmala is recited in every rakʿa.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في كل ركعة، عن أبي يوسف

rows.speaker: محمد
rows.claim: Muḥammad holds that the basmala is recited before each sūra.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عند كل سورة، عن محمد

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala should not be recited aloud.
rows.anchor: واختلفوا فقيل: لا يجهر، عن أبي حنيفة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī holds that it should be recited aloud.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يجهر، عن الشافعي

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas says he heard neither the Prophet nor Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar recite the basmala aloud in prayer.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس (صليت خلف رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وخلف أبي بكر وعمر فلم أسمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard reading has ḥamd with a nominative dāl and li-llāh with kasra on lām; al-Ḥasan reads dāl with kasra, while Ibrāhīm b. Abī ʿAbla reads both letters with ḍamma by vowel-following.
rows.anchor: القراءة الظاهرة برفع الدال (لله) بكسر اللام، وعن الحسن أنه قرأ بكسر الدال

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows kasra on the dāl or ḍamma on the lām by vowel-following, but most grammarians reject it as destroying inflection and because following across words is weak; only widely transmitted readings are valid.
rows.anchor: وعن الفراء جواز كسر الدال على الإتباع، وجواز ضم اللام على الإتباع

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: A nominative-style report from Zayd b. ʿAlī on the bāʾ of rabb is only proof of grammatical possibility, not a canonical reading.
rows.anchor: وروي عن زيد بن علي نصب الباء، ويحمل على أنه بين جوازه، لا أنه قراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All reciters agree on kasra for the bāʾ in rabb.
rows.anchor: وأجمع القراء على كسر الباء في (رب)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd, praise, and gratitude are near-synonyms, but praise may answer to blessing or other good, whereas gratitude is only for a blessing; their opposites are blame and ingratitude respectively.
rows.anchor: وبين الحمد والشكر فرق؛ لأن نقيض الحمد الذم، ونقيض الشكر الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss defines praise and gratitude as acknowledging a benefactor’s blessings while believing in His greatness; gratitude is primarily of the heart, and may be required verbally when denial is suspected.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معنى الحمد والشكر: الاعتراف بنعم المنعم مع اعتقاد بعظمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd fundamentally means describing someone with what is beautiful; it is a verbal noun with no dual or plural.
rows.anchor: وأصل الحمد: الوصف بالجميل، والحمد مصدر لا يثنى ولا يجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can mean master, owner, or nurturer/reformer, from the idea of upbringing.
rows.anchor: والرب: السيد، والرب: المالك، والرب: المربي المصلح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأبي علي
rows.claim: Al-ʿālamīn may derive from knowledge, from a sign of its maker, or denote the rational kinds—angels, jinn, and humans—according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū ʿAlī.
rows.anchor: والعالمين: واحدها عالم، وقيل: اشتقاقه من العلم؛ لأنه اسم يقع على ما يعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations make al-ʿālamīn the people of each age or everything contained by the celestial sphere; it has no singular from the same word-form, like qawm and rahṭ.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أهل كل زمان عالم، وقيل: هو اسم لما حواه الفلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥamd is chosen instead of al-shukr because praise applies to blessings and other things: God is praised both for favors and for His good acts and lofty attributes.
rows.anchor: لأن الحمد يكون على نعمة وغير نعمة، فنحن نحمده على نعمته علينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause al-ḥamdu li-llāh is formally a statement with the force of a command to praise God; one estimate supplies “say,” making it accusative.
rows.anchor: الحمد لله خبر ومعناه الأمر، كأنه قال: احمدوا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “I say: praise belongs to God” allows nominative by treating praise as an initial subject; Arabic also permits accusative by supplying “make the praise for God.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: أقول: الحمد لله، فعلى هذا يحتمل الرفع بتقدير ابتدائي الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb is kasra as an adjective of God, though accusative or nominative is also possible for praise.
rows.anchor: وكسر رب، لأنه جعل صفة لله تعالى، ولو نصب أو رفع جاز على المدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The article in al-ḥamd is generic: all praise and thanks belong to God because all blessings come from Him.
rows.anchor: والألف واللام للجنس، يعني كل الحمد لله؛ لأن النعم كلها منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb al-ʿālamīn means either master and owner of creation or their originator and nurturer.
rows.anchor: قيل: سيد الخلق ومالكهم، وقيل: منشئهم ومربيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Raḥmān gives the blessings of worldly life and religion; al-Raḥīm has expansive mercy, and the whole praise belongs to the One who creates, owns, blesses, and deserves worship.
rows.anchor: المنعم بنعم الدنيا والدين. الرحيم: واسع الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Explanations for repeating al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm: the first occurrence is outside the sūra, it first seeks aid and the second assigns praise to God, or the repetition emphasizes mercy.
rows.anchor: قيل: لأن الأول ليس من السورة

rows.speaker: علي بن عيسى
rows.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā denies mere repetition: the first occurrence links servitude to blessings warranting worship, the second links praise to blessings warranting praise.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse makes praise and gratitude for God’s blessings obligatory and teaches worshippers how to praise Him.
rows.anchor: الآية تدل على وجوب الحمد لله، والشكر على نعمه، وفيه تعليم منه لعباده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person fulfills the duty of gratitude by doing what is within his capacity; gratitude encompasses past and future blessings, which are known collectively, so it is owed collectively.
rows.anchor: إذا أتى بما في وسعه فقد أدى حق الشكر، ولأن شكره يتناول النعم الماضية والآتية

rows.speaker: أبو بكر وعاصم والكسائي ويعقوب
rows.claim: Abū Bakr, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, and Yaʿqūb read Mālik with an alif; this is also transmitted from the four caliphs and many early Muslims.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو بكر وعاصم والكسائي ويعقوب مالك بالألف، وهي قراءة الخلفاء الأربعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining reciters read Malik without an alif; both forms are well-known readings transmitted from the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والباقون بغير ألف، وكلاهما مرويان عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view prefers Malik because kingship entails grandeur and command over many, while one may own only a small thing; malik also encompasses mulk and milk.
rows.anchor: فقيل: ملك أمدح؛ لأنه لا يكون إلا مع التعظيم والاحتواء على الجمع الكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view prefers Mālik because it includes kingship and ownership: an owner necessarily possesses what he owns, whereas a king may rule what he does not possess; its extra alif adds force.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مالك أمدح؛ لأنه يتناول الملك، ولقوله: (قل اللهم مالك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noncanonical forms such as Malik with a vowelless lām or Mālik as vocative or nominative may be Arabic but are not valid recitations.
rows.anchor: وإن كان جائزا في العربية فلا تجوز القراءة به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two words are associated with strength/binding, supported by a line of poetry, or with power; a king can dispose of what is his, while an owner has broad capacity for policy and administration.
rows.anchor: وأصله من الاشتقاق من الشد والربط، ومنه قول الشاعر: ملكت بها كفي فأنهرت فتقها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm usually means daylight from sunrise to sunset but may mean any period; Resurrection Day is named for the interval until judgment ends and each group settles in its abode.
rows.anchor: ويستعمل بمعنى الوقت، يقال: أيام بني العباس، وسمي يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي
rows.claim: Al-dīn is glossed as the Day of Reckoning by Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī.
rows.anchor: يوم الحساب، عن ابن عباس والسدي

rows.speaker: الضحاك وقتادة
rows.claim: Al-Daḥḥāk and Qatāda gloss al-dīn as recompense.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يوم الجزاء، عن الضحاك، وقتادة

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī connects the Day of Recompense with dīn as recompense.
rows.anchor: عن الدين، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other glosses call it the Day of domination, from dāntuhu (I subdued you), or the day when only religion benefits, from Muḥammad b. Kaʿb.
rows.anchor: يوم القهر، من قولهم: دينته أي قهرته، وقيل: يوم لا ينفع إلا الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik is genitive as an adjective of God; Arabic can also treat it as a vocative or an initial nominative, and yawm is genitive by annexation.
rows.anchor: مكسور الكاف؛ لأنه نعت لله، ويجوز في العربية نصب الكاف على النداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing God’s lordship over creation and kingship in this world, the verse declares His authority over the Hereafter; Mālik means the One able over Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: لما بين تعالى أنه رب العالمين، وملك الدنيا بين ملكه في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse affirms resurrection and offers encouragement and warning, since imagining the final day gives the morally responsible person both hope and fear.
rows.anchor: الآية تدل على إثبات المعاد، وعلى ترغيب وترهيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view treats Malik and Mālik as equivalent because the day is not yet existent, so both indicate God’s power over it; another distinguishes kingship of the day from the day’s being under His power.
rows.anchor: وقيل: دلالة ملك ومالك واحدة؛ لأن اليوم معدوم، فمعناه القدرة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has kasra on the first vowel of iyyāka and fatḥa on the first nūn of nastaʿīn; another Arabic dialect is possible but not an accepted reading.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة (إياك) بكسر الألف، (ونستعين) بفتح النون الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyāka is derived as iwyāka, with wāw changed and assimilated into yāʾ, and is associated with seeking refuge; as a detached pronoun it precedes its verb unless a separator intervenes.
rows.anchor: أصله إوياك، قلبت الواو ياء وأدغمت في الياء، فصار إياك

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abū Ḥātim classifies iyyāka as a detached pronoun, as opposed to connected or implicit pronouns.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حاتم: إياك ضمير منفصل، والضمير ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second kind of divine assistance brings a person closer to doing a duty or choosing it, as with divine لطف; it belongs to one known to have such help and may precede or accompany action.
rows.anchor: المعلوم أن له لطفا، ثم اللطف قد يتقدم الفعل وقد يقارنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though assistance from God is obligatory in this account, asking for it remains meaningful: one who knows an act is good wants help to do it, and supplication can itself be worship or a لطف occasioned by the request.
rows.anchor: من علم حسن فعل أحب أن يعان عليه، ولأن الطلب قد يكون عبادة وإن كان واجبا

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza reads ṣirāṭ with an articulation between ṣād and zāy throughout the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة الصراط بإشمام الصاد الزاي كل القرآن

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī is reported to articulate ṣirāṭ with an articulation between sīn and ṣād throughout the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وعن الكسائي بإشمام السين كل القرآن

rows.speaker: يعقوب برواية رويس
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb in Ruways’s narration reads ṣirāṭ with sīn throughout the Qur’an; attribution of that reading to Ibn Kathīr is said to be mistaken.
rows.anchor: قرأ يعقوب برواية رويس بالسين كل القرآن، وقرأ الآخرون بالصاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers ṣād: it better harmonizes with emphatic ṭāʾ, is Qurashī, matches the written codex, and is the reading of most leading reciters; the other forms retain or suggest the root or harmonize voicing.
rows.anchor: والاختيار الصاد لوجوه: منها: أن اجتماع الحرفين المتشاكلين أحسن في المسموع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance linguistically is indication or direction along a way, opposite error, and in essence indicates the truth; ṣirāṭ means path, from the image of swallowing food, and istiqāmah resembles evenness, opposite crookedness.
rows.anchor: أصل الهداية في اللغة الدلالة، يقال: هديته إلى الطريق، أي دللته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ihdinā the object pronoun is the first object, ṣirāṭ the second, and al-mustaqīm modifies ṣirāṭ.
rows.anchor: والصراط: المفعول الثاني، والمستقيم: نعت للصراط

rows.speaker: أبي علي وأبي بن كعب
rows.claim: One gloss asks God to keep the worshippers firm on the straight way of guidance, like telling someone already eating to continue eating.
rows.anchor: قيل: ثبتنا على الطريق المستقيم والهداية، عن أبي علي وأبي بن كعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other proposed meanings ask for direction to Paradise in the Hereafter, future divine لطف to dispel doubts and satanic whispering even for believers, or direction to the route to success and deliverance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أرشدنا إلى طريق الجنة في الآخرة، وقيل: الطف بنا في المستقبل والمستأنف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request to be kept on the path is best because it matches the preceding request for assistance.
rows.anchor: والأحسن هو الأول؛ ليشاكل ما قبله من طلب المعونة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse requires asking God for guidance and teaches worshippers how to pray; it also calls for repeated supplication so desires do not lead them astray.
rows.anchor: الآية تدل على وجوب طلب الهداية، وتعليم من الله كيف ندعوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author argues human acts are not created by God: otherwise requesting help and guidance would be pointless, like asking help for one’s colors or bodily form.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أن أفعال العباد ليست بخلق لله

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza reads the hāʾ in ʿalayhim, ilayhim, and ladayhim with ḍamma throughout the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة: (عليهم) و(إليهم) و(لديهم) بضم الهاء

rows.speaker: يعقوب
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb gives ḍamma to each hāʾ preceded by a vowelless yāʾ, including forms such as ʿalayhim and fīhim, and reportedly also where that yāʾ drops.
rows.anchor: وعن يعقوب ضم كل هاء قبلها ياء ساكنة، ك (عليهم)، و(إليهم)، و(فيهم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers vary between kasra and ḍamma on the hāʾ, and between a vowelless, kasra, or ḍamma mīm of the plural, especially before a following hamzat al-waṣl; the author lists each school’s distributions.
rows.anchor: فأما من ضم الهاء، فلأنه يردها إلى الأصل، لأنك تقول: أعطيتموه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍamma on hāʾ restores its underlying form; kasra is influenced by the preceding yāʾ, avoiding a heavy shift from ḍamma beside yāʾ, while ḍamma on mīm restores its base and appended wāw lengthens it.
rows.anchor: ومن كسرها فلأجل الياء الساكنة. ومن كسر الهاء وجزم الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inʿām, iḥsān, and ifḍāl are near-synonyms, though one may act beneficently toward oneself but cannot bless oneself; niʿma derives from softness and denotes good intended benefit.
rows.anchor: الإنعام والإحسان والإفضال نظائر، وبين الإنعام والإحسان فرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God blesses both believers and unbelievers; His first favor to a servant is creating that person alive for benefit.
rows.anchor: والله منعم على المؤمن والكافر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the sūra is Meccan; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says it is Medinan, and it is called Sūrat al-Aʿlā.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنها مكية، عن ابن عباس. وقيل: مدنية، عن الضحاك. وسميت سورة (الأعلى)

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy transmits the Prophet’s promise that reciting al-Aʿlā earns ten good deeds for each letter revealed to Abraham, Moses, and Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وعن النبي صلى الله عليه فيما رواه أبي: من قرأ سورة (الأعلى) أعطاه الله من الأجر

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports that the Prophet loved this sūra and that Michael was the first to say “Glory to my Lord, the Most High.”
rows.anchor: وعن علي: كان رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - يحب هذه السورة (سبح اسم ربك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet through Gabriel promises an immense scale-weight and forgiveness and Paradise for saying the phrase in or outside prayer.
rows.anchor: يا جبريل، أخبرني عن ثواب من قالها في صلاته أو غير صلاته؟

rows.speaker: عقبة بن عامر
rows.claim: ʿUqba b. ʿĀmir reports that the Prophet assigned “Glorify the name of your Lord, the Great” to bowing and this verse to prostration; similar reports come from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn al-Zubayr.
rows.anchor: وعن عقبة بن عامر قال: لما نزل قوله: (فسبح باسم ربك العظيم)

rows.speaker: جويبر
rows.claim: Juwaybir reports from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said this phrase in prostration and directed anyone reciting the sūra to say it likewise.
rows.anchor: وعن جويبر، عن الضحاك أنه كان يقول ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ويعقوب وقتيبة عن الكسائي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, and Qutayba from al-Kisāʾī read yuʾthirūn in the third person, referring to al-ashqā; other readers use the direct-address reading, preferred because it is Ubayy’s reading and most readers follow it.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو ويعقوب وقتيبة عن الكسائي: يؤثرون بالياء كناية عن الأشقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reminder means explaining so that understanding produces recollection, and its benefit is great because it leads to needed knowledge.
rows.anchor: التذكير: التعريض للذكر بالبيان الذي يقع به الفهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sayadhakkaru derives from sayatadhakkaru, with the tāʾ assimilated into the adjacent dhāl.
rows.anchor: أصله [سيذتكر]، فأدغم التاء في الذال لقرب مخرجهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tajannub is turning to one side, away from something that conflicts with it; shaqwa is a condition leading to severe punishment, opposite felicity.
rows.anchor: والتجنب: المصير في جانب من الشيء بما ينافي غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falāḥ, success, and gain are near-synonyms for attaining one’s goal.
rows.anchor: والفلاح والنجاح والغنم نظائر، وهو الظفر بالبغية

rows.speaker: أبي العالية وأبي سعيد الخدري وابن عمر
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and Ibn ʿUmar connect purification with the alms of fast-breaking and the Eid prayer; Ibn ʿUmar would check that Nafiʿ had paid before leaving for prayer.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية، وأبي سعيد الخدري، وابن عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is commanded to deliver the Qur’an and admonish with its promises, warnings, and rulings; “if the reminder benefits” need not impose a condition, since it certainly increases obedience and curbs sin.
rows.anchor: فذكر أي: أد إليهم القرآن، وعظهم به، وذكرهم ما فيه من الوعد والوعيد والأحكام

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the Prophet must deliver his universal mission whether people accept it or not, so the proof is established.
rows.anchor: عن أبي علي قال: لأنه مبعوث إلى الكافة، فيجب أن يؤدي

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim reads the instruction as admonishing when one hopes the listeners will benefit and their hearts are receptive.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المراد إن رجوت فيهم الانتفاع، وأملت قلوبهم، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing unbelievers after commands to obey, the author explains that they choose and work for worldly life rather than reflect on the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: بل تؤثرون تختارون الحياة الدنيا فتعملون لها، وتعمرونها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hereafter is better and more lasting because worldly pleasure is slight, interrupted, and mixed with annoyances, while the next life’s pleasure endures unspoiled.
rows.anchor: لأن نعيم الدنيا قليل وينقطع، ومشوب بكل منغص

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says “this” in “this is in the earlier scriptures” means the entire sūra and everything stated in it.
rows.anchor: قيل: أراد جميع السورة، وما نص فيها، عن قتادة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says “this” means the passage from “successful is the one who purifies himself” to the sūra’s end.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد قوله: (قد أفلح من تزكى) إلى آخر السورة، عن الكلبي

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd takes “this” to mean that the Hereafter is better and more enduring.
rows.anchor: يعني قوله: والآخرة خير وأبقى، عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk takes “this” to mean the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا القرآن، عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī understands the earlier-scripture reference as God’s admonition and explanation urging preference for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: ما وعظكم به وبينه لكم لتؤثروا الآخرة على الدنيا، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations identify “this” as the admonition to obey and avoid sin, the praised status of purification and prayer in earlier scriptures, or the commands given to the communities addressed by their scriptures (Abū Muslim).
rows.anchor: معناه: هذا الذي ذكرناك ووعظناك به، والترغيب في الطاعة، والنهي عن المعصية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier scriptures are the books of Abraham and Moses.
rows.anchor: الصحف الأولى أي: كتب الأولين صحف إبراهيم وموسى كتابهما

rows.speaker: أبي ذر
rows.claim: Abū Dharr asked the Prophet what the earlier scriptures contained; the Prophet answered by reciting these two verses.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي ذر، قلت: يا رسول الله، ما كان في الصحف الأولى؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One saying attributed to Abraham’s scriptures advises the rational person to guard his tongue, know his time, and attend to his own affairs; the author also says 104 books were revealed to a list of prophets.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في صحف إبراهيم: (ينبغي للعاقل أن يكون حافظا للسانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to remind establishes the obligation of remembrance and calling people to God.
rows.anchor: يدل قوله: فذكر على وجوب التذكر والدعاء إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wretched person’s turning away is his own act and he can do otherwise, so it is blameworthy; this refutes the determinists’ doctrine of created human acts and capacity.
rows.anchor: أن التجنب فعله، وأنه يقدر على خلافه؛ لذلك صح ذمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise is attained through the combined deeds named: purification consists of performing obligations and avoiding grave sins; purification, prayer, and remembrance are human actions.
rows.anchor: والتطهير إنما يحصل بأداء الواجبات واجتناب الكبائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct address “you prefer” shows that choosing worldly life is an act of its human subjects.
rows.anchor: ويدل قوله: (بل تؤثرون) أن اختيارهم ذلك فعلهم

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reports the Prophet’s promise that reciting al-Ghāshiya will bring an easy reckoning from God.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال: من قرأ سورة (الغاشية)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra opens by explaining the Hereafter and the destinies of believers and those who preferred worldly life, extending the prior sūra’s conclusion that the Hereafter is better, as encouragement and warning.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم سورة (سبح) بأن الآخرة خير من الأولى، افتتح هذه السورة ببيان أحوال الآخرة

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ويعقوب وأبو بكر عن عاصم
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Yaʿqūb, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read taṣlā with passive ḍamma, matching tusqā; the rest read it with fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو ويعقوب وأبو بكر عن عاصم: تصلى بضم التاء على ما لم يسم فاعله

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read lā tusmaʿ with a passive ḍamma and lāghiyah nominative; Nāfiʿ instead has direct-address fatḥa and accusative lāghiyah.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب: لا تسمع بالتاء مضمومة، لاغية بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hal can introduce a question of denial or a report meant to magnify something; a poet’s question illustrates asking for grandeur despite already knowing.
rows.anchor: (هل) حرف استفهام، ثم يذكر، ويراد به الإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ghāshiya is what envelops an object on every side; its root connotes covering or veiling.
rows.anchor: والغاشية: ما أحاط بالشيء من جميع جهاته، وأصله: الستر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khushūʿ means abasement, submission, and melancholy.
rows.anchor: والخشوع: الذل والخضوع والكآبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāṣibah or nuṣbah means exhaustion, particularly weakness brought on by exertion.
rows.anchor: والناصبة والنصبة: التعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣalāʾ may mean adhering to the fire permanently or burning fuel; ḥāmiyah means hot.
rows.anchor: والصلاء: اللزوم، ومنه: الاصطلاء من يلزم النار للأبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āniyah is water at the peak of heat; the root means reaching maturity or the appointed time, as in the Qur’anic phrase about food reaching its time.
rows.anchor: والآنية: البالغة شدة الحر ونهايته، وأصله البلوغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍarīʿ is a plant eaten by camels that harms but does not benefit them; they mistake it for other plants, and its name suggests resemblance.
rows.anchor: والضريع: نبت تأكله الإبل يضر، ولا ينفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laghw, lāghiyah, and lawāghī mean speech without benefit; a poetic line is cited as evidence for the word laghw.
rows.anchor: اللغو واللاغية واللواغي: كلام لا فائدة فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wujūh begins a nominal sentence with khāshiʿah as its predicate; ʿāmilah modifies wujūh.
rows.anchor: وجوه ابتداء، وخبره: خاشعة. عاملة نعت له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Quraysh objected that their camels fattened on ḍarīʿ, the verse “it neither fattens nor relieves hunger” was revealed in reply.
rows.anchor: قالت كفار قريش: إن إبلنا تسمن من الضريع، فنزل: (لا يسمن ولا يغني من جوع)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة وأبو علي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Abū ʿAlī take al-ghāshiya as the Resurrection, enveloping people in terrors; the question magnifies its importance and hal may mean “already.”
rows.anchor: هل أتاك حديث الغاشية قيل: هل بلغك خبر القيامة

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says al-ghāshiya is the particular event that befalls people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ما يرد عليهم بعينه، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Muḥammad b. Kaʿb and Saʿīd b. Jubayr identify al-ghāshiya with Hell, which covers unbelievers’ faces in punishment.
rows.anchor: الغاشية النار تغشى وجوه الكفار بالعذاب، كقوله: (وتغشى وجوههم النار)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wujūh may mean the leading people of a group or the literal facial organs; yawm idh is Resurrection Day, and another gloss places them in Hell.
rows.anchor: أراد أرباب الوجوه، كقولهم: جاءني وجوه القوم، أي: ساداتهم

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وسعيد بن جبير والضحاك
rows.claim: A group including al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say the people labored in Hell with chains and shackles because they had not worked for God in this life; Ibn ʿAbbās reports something similar.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن، وقتادة، وسعيد بن جبير، والضحاك، وروي نحوه عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says they are made to climb a mountain of iron in Hell.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: يكلفون ارتقاء جبل من حديد في النار

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says they fall onto their faces in Hell.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: يخرون على وجوههم في النار

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says they arrogantly refused obedience in worldly life, so they labor and exhaust themselves in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: تكبرت في الدنيا عن طاعة الله، فأعملها وأنصبها في الآخرة

rows.speaker: عكرمة والسدي
rows.claim: ʿIkrima and al-Suddī read the phrase as people who committed sins in this life and are exhausted in Hell in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة، والسدي

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says some exerted themselves in worldly acts hoping for good, but their work was outside God’s commands and instead involved prohibitions, so they deserve Hell.
rows.anchor: عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading pictures them being dragged toward Hell and exhausted by the dragging and severe torment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عاملة يجرونها إلى النار، ناصبة في جرها، وشدة عذابها

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Saʿīd b. Jubayr and Zayd b. Aslam identify them as monks, recluses, and innovators whose works become futile and who enter Hell.
rows.anchor: فأعمالهم تصير هباء، ويدخلون النار، عن سعيد ين جبير، وزيد بن أسلم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says they are laboring as they are driven to Hell on the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سائرة ناصبة في القيامة، تساق إلى النار، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These explanations need not conflict: the accepted person works for God on the truth and is pleased with the effort, while other labor is fruitless and leaves its burden or sin.
rows.anchor: ولا تنافي بين الجميع فيحمل عليها، كأنه قيل: كل من كان على الحق يعمل لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessed faces and their satisfaction with their labor contrast with the futile efforts just described.
rows.anchor: ويدل قولة: (وجوه) على أحوال المؤمن، ورضاه بعمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage describes what is prepared for both groups.
rows.anchor: وتدل الآيات على ما أعد للفريقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the faces “working” and referring to “their effort” proves that human acts belong to their human agents, against determinism.
rows.anchor: وتدل على أن أعمال العباد فعلهم؛ لذلك قال: (عاملة)، وقال: (لسعيها)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jāriyah first describes liquid flowing quickly, then horses or ships; a running spring is more attractive than a still one and thus suits Paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي العين الجارية من الحسن والميعة ما ليس في الواقفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surur is the plural of sarīr, a seat associated with joy and elevation.
rows.anchor: والسرر: جمع سرير، وهو مجلس السرور والرفعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Akwaab are cups or pitchers without spouts; another gloss says they lack both handles and spouts and are fine, beautiful drinking vessels.
rows.anchor: والأكواب: جمع كوب، وهي الأباريق ليس لها خراطيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Namāriq is the plural of nimriqah, with either ḍamma or kasra on both nūn and rāʾ.
rows.anchor: والنمارق: واحدها: نمرقة، وفيه لغتان بضم النون والراء، وكسرهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mabthūthah means scattered; the Qur’anic phrase “spread through it every kind of animal” shares the root, while al-bath is grief that disperses the heart.
rows.anchor: والمبثوثة: المتفرقة، ومنه: (وبث فيها من كل دابة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Musayṭir means one who controls another by coercion; it derives from writing, since keepers and overseers preserve matters in writing.
rows.anchor: المسيطر: المتسلط على غيره بالقهر له، وسيطر: تسلط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyāb means returning, as shown by the related verbal forms listed.
rows.anchor: والإياب: الرجوع، آب أوبا وإيابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Except one who turns away” can be a disconnected exception meaning “but”; Abū Muslim prefers the sense “rather, one who turns away.”
rows.anchor: استثناء منقطع، معناه: لكن من تولى، قال أبو مسلم: معناه: بل من تولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other syntax connects the exception to “you are not a controller”: the Prophet would control the one who turned away through fighting until conversion, after which God punishes him.
rows.anchor: إلا من تولى فإنك مسيطر عليهم بالجهاد حتى يسلموا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another construction connects the exception to “remind”: admonish your people except those who turn away and will not benefit from the reminder.
rows.anchor: هو راجع إلى قوله: (فذكر) قومك إلا من تولى وأعرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes say that when unbelievers were astonished and denied the Paradise just described, God recalled His power through His creation and revealed the signs passage.
rows.anchor: عجب الكفار وكذبوا بها، فذكرهم الله قدرته بصنعه

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim links the signs to the opening: the pronoun in “do they look?” refers back to the futile workers; after describing punishment and reward, God argues from creation to His wise authorship and the duty to worship Him.
rows.anchor: والضمير في قوله: (ينظرون) راجع إلى (عاملة) لم ينفعهم عملهم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: A second coherence view says listeners wondered how to climb the lofty couches; God points to the huge but docile camel, and to the raised sky, spread earth, and firmly set mountains.
rows.anchor: وقالوا: كيف نصعد عليها؟ فأراهم الإبل كيف تركب مع عظمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has ʿĀd with nunation, while al-Ḥasan annexes “Iram” without nunation; Iram is normally read with kasra, but Mujāhid opens it.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة: بعاد منونا، وقرأ الحسن: (بعاد إرم) على الإضافة من غير تنوين

rows.speaker: المؤرج
rows.claim: Al-Muʾarrij explains open Iram as resembling the plural āram, signs or landmarks; aram can also mean destruction, as in a clan perishing.
rows.anchor: قال المؤرج: من قرأ بفتح الألف شبيهم بالآرام وهي الأعلام

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ويعقوب
rows.claim: In some transmissions Ibn Kathīr and Yaʿqūb retain the yāʾ in bi-l-wādī in both pause and continuation; Warsh retains it in continuation, as do Abū Jaʿfar and Abū Ḥātim by preference.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير في بعض الرويات عنه ويعقوب: بالوادي بإثبات الياء وصلا ووقفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readers drop the yāʾ in both positions for ease and to match the verse-end rhyme; dropping it at pause reflects the intended stop, while Khalaf from al-Kisāʾī keeps it because the noun is incomplete without it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون بحذفها في الحالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fajr means breaking the column of dawn; two dawns are distinguished: the elongated false dawn remains legally night, but the spreading true dawn governs fasting and prayer.
rows.anchor: الفجر: شق عمود الصبح، فجره الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shafʿ means an even pair and derives from joining; watr is an individual with no counterpart.
rows.anchor: والشفع: الزوج، وأصله من الضم، ومنه: الشفيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥajr derives from restraint: it is an embargo, something forbidden, rock made resistant, or reason that prevents wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: والحجر: أصله المنع، ومنه يقال: حجر القاضي على فلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿImād means the pillars supporting buildings and is extended metaphorically to strength and honor; a poetic line illustrates its use for a household’s support.
rows.anchor: والعماد: جمعه عمد، وهو ما تبنى به الأبنية، وتستعمل في القوة والشرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jawb means cutting through; al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī’s line uses it of crossing the night, and ʿuthumthum describes tall or heavy camels.
rows.anchor: قال النابغة الجعدي: أتاك أبو ليلى يجوب به الدجى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath ending places inn rabbaka la-bi-l-mirṣād as its answer; possible implicit answers include God seizing every tyrant or avenging each wronged person, while another estimate makes God’s creative power the point.
rows.anchor: وجوابه (إن ربك لبالمرصاد) وتقديره: ورب هذه الأشياء ومهلك هذه الأمم

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī takes Iram as an epithet of ʿĀd distinguishing this people from others named ʿĀd; al-Ḥasan and Abū Muslim instead call it another name for ʿĀd.
rows.anchor: فقيل: إرم صفة لعاد، وكان عاد يعرف به ويوصف به ليتميز به من غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations make Iram a lofty structure owned by its namesake or derive it from destruction, meaning God reduced the people to ruins.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إرم: بنيان بناؤه رفيع البنيان، فأضيف إليه كأنه قيل: صاحب إرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading best supports Abū ʿAlī’s and Abū Muslim’s interpretation of Iram as apposition to ʿĀd.
rows.anchor: وظاهر التلاوة ما قاله أبو علي وأبو مسلم؛ لأن إرم بدل من عاد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid say dhāt al-ʿimād means exceptionally tall; al-Kalbī says each person was 400 cubits high, whereas Muqātil says twelve cubits.
rows.anchor: قيل: ذات الطول، عن ابن عباس، ومجاهد. من قول العرب: رجل معمد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says they lived in portable, pole-supported tents and moved from place to place.
rows.anchor: ذات عمد للأبيات ينتقلون من مكان إلى مكان، عن قتادة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets dhāt al-ʿimād as sturdy, well-constructed buildings.
rows.anchor: ذات العماد في إحكام البنيان، عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk interprets the phrase as their strong, forceful power; a raised report describes a man lifting a rock onto a community to kill them.
rows.anchor: ذات القوى الشداد، عن الضحاك وروي مرفوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says they had gardens and crops and lived in Wādī al-Qurā.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كانت لهم جنات وزروع، وكانوا يسكنون بوادي القرى

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبي علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAlī describe them as builders of enormous, high structures.
rows.anchor: ذات الأبنية العظام المرتفعة، عن الحسن، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iram dhāt al-ʿimād is also said to be the garden built by Shaddād b. ʿĀd, whom God killed before he could enter; Abū Muslim explains the phrase as height and strength.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إرم ذات العماد هو الجنة التي بناها شداد بن عاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No people like ʿĀd were created in the land in bodily size and strength, yet their power could not protect them when they disobeyed God.
rows.anchor: مثل عاد في عظم أجسامهم وكثرة قوتهم، ثم ذلك لم يغنهم عن عذاب الله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says the Thamūd cut rock, or cut mountains into houses; they lived in their valley or Wādī al-Qurā, built structures there, and were said to be first to carve stone.
rows.anchor: قوم صالح الذين جابوا قيل: قطعوا الصخر وقيل: قطعوا الجبال بيوتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The placement of the account of ʿĀd and Thamūd within the oath poses no problem if its answer is implicit; if the answer is “your Lord is watching,” their destruction joins the oath as evidence, or the answer may be that every wrongdoer will be seized as they were.
rows.anchor: ومن قال الجواب قوله: (إن ربك لبالمرصاد) يقول: لهذا الكلام تعلق بالقسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dawn oath and what follows highlight the great value of these signs and blessings as evidence for the Creator.
rows.anchor: يدل قوله: (والفجر) وما بعده على عظيم موقع هذه الأشياء من النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The downfall of ʿĀd, Thamūd, and Pharaoh despite their strength and wealth warns people against disobeying God and becoming deluded by worldly life, self, power, or armies.
rows.anchor: يغن عنهم شيئا حين عصوه، تحذيرا من عصيان الله تعالى، والاغترار بالدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar read qaddara with a doubled dāl; others read it light, with different glosses for restricting or allotting sufficient provision.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر وأبو جعفر: قدر عليه رزقه بتشديد الدال، الباقون بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr says the doubled reading means straitening provision, while the light reading means giving enough; another view gives both forms the meaning “restricted.”
rows.anchor: وكان أبو عمرو يقول: قدر مشددة بمعنى قتر، وقدر مخففة: هو أن يعطيه ما يكفيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both forms derive from measuring: God sets livelihood at subsistence; capability also derives from a measured extent of what can be brought into being.
rows.anchor: وأصله من: القدر، وهو كون الشيء بمقدار

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar and Nāfiʿ retain the yāʾ of akramanī and ahānanī in continuation but drop it at pause.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر ونافع: أكرمني وأهانني بإثبات الياء في الوصل وحذفها في الوقف

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ويعقوب
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and Yaʿqūb preserve the two yāʾs both in continuation and pause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ويعقوب بإثبات الياء فيهما على الحالين

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr permits either retaining or dropping the two yāʾs in both positions.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو بإثباتهما وحذفهما في الحالين

rows.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī drop both yāʾs in either position for ease and to follow the codex, while retention follows the original form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي بحذف الياء في الحرفين في الحالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb use fatḥa on the yāʾs in rabbī akramanī and ahānanī; the others use sukūn.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر ونافع وابن كثير وأبو عمرو ويعقوب: ربي أكرمني وربي أهانني بفتح الياء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb read the four verbs “honor,” “urge,” “eat,” and “love” in the third person; others address the listeners directly.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو ويعقوب الأربعة كلها بالياء

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī read taḥāḍḍūn with alif as reciprocal urging—people urging one another.
rows.anchor: فقرأ أبو جعفر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي: تحاضون بفتح التاء والألف

rows.speaker: نافع وابن كثير وابن عامر
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Ibn ʿĀmir read taḥuḍḍūn without an alif.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن كثير وابن عامر: تحضون بالتاء وضم الحاء من غير ألف

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb use the third-person yāʾ form without alif; al-Kisāʾī is also reported with a ḍamma on tāʾ and an alif.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو ويعقوب بالياء وضم الحاء بغير ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Watad is a peg; the plural is awtād, as in the phrase calling mountains pegs.
rows.anchor: الوتد: جمعه: أوتاد، ومنه: (والجبال أوتادا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭughyān means exceeding the limit in corruption, like water going beyond its boundary.
rows.anchor: والطغيان: مجاوزة الحد في الإفساد، ومنه: (طغى الماء)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says sawṭ can name a share of punishment even when no whip is involved; the author also links the word with mixing and cites poetry for that usage.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: السوط اسم للعذاب وإن لم يكن ثم ضرب بسوط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirṣād is an instrument noun from watching or lying in wait; the text glosses it as a watcher.
rows.anchor: والمرصاد: مفعال من: رصده يرصده رصدا فهو راصد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Testing, trying, and examining are equivalent terms; divine testing brings out the good or evil already known in a servant amid competing calls of reason, law, guidance, and Satan.
rows.anchor: والابتلاء والاختبار والامتحان نظائر، وهو من الله تعالى إظهار ما في العبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikrām is giving something good for its beneficial use, synonymous with iḥsān and inʿām and opposite to humiliating.
rows.anchor: والإكرام إعطاء الخير للانتفاع به، ونظيره: الإحسان والإنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lamm means gathering: a person who lamma the food eats everything he can reach without distinguishing one item from another.
rows.anchor: واللم: الجمع، يقال: لممت ما على الخوان ألمه لما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jamm means large or abundant; the term describes a great volume of water, with a poetic example for abundant water.
rows.anchor: والجم: الكبير العظيم، يقال لمعظم الماء: جمة الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative of aklan is an absolute object and lammā modifies the eating.
rows.anchor: أكلا نصب على المصدر وهو المفعول المطلق، ولما نعت للأكل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transition from God’s watchfulness to human misinterpretation is explained by several views: He watches all deeds and welfare so blessings call for gratitude and hardship for patience (Abū Muslim); He charges people with what serves their welfare before they become subject to earned recompense; or their ignorance mistakes welfare for honor or humiliation.
rows.anchor: قلنا: فيه وجوه: أحدها: أنه بالمرصاد لأعمالهم، ولهم، لا يخفى عليه شيء من مصالحهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke “rather, you do not honor” answers the claim that restricted provision means God is humiliating people: their own neglect is the fault.
rows.anchor: لما رد عليهم ظنهم أن التقدير الإهانة، بين أن الإهانة لهذا، لا لما قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage is said to have been revealed about Umayya b. Khalaf, who mistook being blessed for esteem without gratitude, and restricted provision for contempt.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزل قوله: (فأما الإنسان) في أمية بن خلف، امتحنه الله بالنعمة

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: In a long sermon Zayd b. ʿAlī prayed that the Banū Abī al-ʿĀṣ, who had transgressed and corrupted the land, be struck with punishment, for God watches them.
rows.anchor: أبي العاص طغوا في البلاد فأكثروا فيها الفساد، اللهم صب عليهم سوط عذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People mistakenly regard prosperity as divine honor and hardship as humiliation; actual recompense is in the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: فيظن النعمة كرامة وجزاء، والمحنة إهانة، جهلا منه، وإنما الجزاء في يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command not to dishonor orphans requires honoring them and caring for their persons and property; they are singled out because their weakness makes them dependent.
rows.anchor: على وجوب إكرام اليتيم، وحسن رعايته في نفسه وماله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes an obligation to protect the rights of the poor.
rows.anchor: ويدل على وجوب رعاية حق الفقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You love” censures someone whose desires are confined to worldly possessions.
rows.anchor: ويدل قوله: وتحبون على ذم من قصر هواه على الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eating, loving, honoring, and urging are human acts, as shown by the praise and blame attached to them.
rows.anchor: ويدل أن هذا الأكل والحب والإكرام والحض فعل العبد

rows.speaker: الكسائي ويعقوب
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read yuʿadhdhib and yūthiq with fatḥa on dhāl and thāʾ; others use kasra, and Abū Qilāba reports the fatḥa reading from someone taught by the Prophet, which Abū ʿAmr later adopted.
rows.anchor: قرأ الكسائي ويعقوب: يعذب بفتح الذال، ولا يوثق بفتح الثاء

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s codex is reported to read “the secure, obedient soul”; another has “among My servant,” and both variants are treated as explanatory readings.
rows.anchor: وروي أن في مصحف أبي: (النفس الآمنة المطيعة)، وعن بعضهم (في عبدي)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakk means leveling a raised surface; an animal’s hump becomes spread flat, as does a dakkān, while another view equates it with shaking until the ground is level.
rows.anchor: الدك: حط المرتفع بالبسط، واندك سنام البعير: إذا انفرش في ظهره

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim treats dakk and rahf as synonyms; a poetic line imagines mountains falling together until every stone is gone.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم: الدك والرحف سواء، قال الشاعر: ليت الجبال تداعت عند مصرعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣaff means objects arranged one after another in an even line, like worshippers in prayer.
rows.anchor: والصف: كون الأشياء بعضها يلي بعضا على خط الاستواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Withāq means binding by a fetter, neck-ring, or chain.
rows.anchor: والوثاق: الشد بمثل القيد والغل والسلاسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muṭmaʾinnah means calm and tranquil.
rows.anchor: المطمئنة: الساكنة، ومنه: الطمأنينة السكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “none punishes with His punishment,” the following noun may be the direct object or mean “like His punishment,” with the preposition omitted; both readings then take accusative.
rows.anchor: أراد مثل عذابه، فلما حذف الخافض نصب

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the verse was revealed concerning Umayya b. Khalaf al-Jumaḥī.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزل قوله: (لا يعذب عذابه أحد) في أمية بن خلف الجمحي، عن الفراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says the “tranquil soul” was revealed about Ḥamza b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib after his martyrdom at Uḥud.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزل قوله: (ياأيتها النفس المطمئنة) في حمزة بن عبد المطلب حين استشهد يوم أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report concerns Khubayb b. ʿAdī, who prayed that God turn his face to the qibla if he had good with Him; God turned it, and no one could turn it back.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزل في خبيب بن عدي لما قتله أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view applies the verse generally to all believers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل الآية عامة في جميع المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā is either a rebuke against unlawful consumption and withholding people’s rights, or means “indeed” according to Abū ʿAlī.
rows.anchor: كلا قيل: ردع وزجر، أي: لا تفعلوا ما أنتم عليه من أكل الحرام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The earth is extended flat like leather on Resurrection Day, according to Ibn ʿAbbās; another gloss has it shaking until all structures disappear.
rows.anchor: تمد الأرض يوم القيامة مد الأديم، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakkan dakkan describes this happening repeatedly until everything on the earth’s surface is broken.
rows.anchor: يفعل ذلك مرة بعد مرة حتى ينكسر كل شيء على ظهرها

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبي علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAlī gloss “your Lord comes” as His command, judgment, and reckoning.
rows.anchor: أمره وقضاؤه ومحاسبته، عن الحسن، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the coming God’s great signs, described as His own coming for magnification; the author rejects a bodily arrival because God is not a body and cannot move.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز حمله على مجيء ذاته؛ لأنه ليس بجسم، فلا يجوز عليه المجيء والذهاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other interpretations say His punishment and reward arrive, or that His command alone appears on Resurrection Day, unlike the worldly situation (Abū Muslim).
rows.anchor: وقيل: جاء عذابه وثوابه، وقيل: جاء أمره الذي لا أمر لغيره معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels stand in aligned ranks for judgment, adding joy to believers and grief to sinners as their deeds are exposed publicly.
rows.anchor: مصطفون في القيامة للحساب، وذلك يزيد في سرور المؤمنين، وغم العصاة

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم وأبي علي
rows.claim: Hell is brought near so people can see its punishments; Abū Muslim and Abū ʿAlī say it was not absent and then newly brought into existence.
rows.anchor: تقرب من الناس، فيرونها وأنواع عذابها، وليس ذلك بغائب، فيحضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation moves Hell’s location closer to where people can see it; the author rejects the Hashwiyya claim that Hell is dragged in chains.
rows.anchor: فأما ما تهذي به الحشوية أنها تقاد بالسلاسل فليس بشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that day people remember their evil deeds, neglect of duties, and wasted time, regret their choices, and wish they had worked to ransom themselves.
rows.anchor: يتذكر الإنسان أفعاله القبيحة، وتركه الواجبات، واشتغاله بما لا ينفعه تندما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question “how could he be reminded?” means remembrance cannot benefit him after obligation ends; alternatively, how will it help after his failures in worldly life?
rows.anchor: أنى له ذكر ينتفع به مع ارتفاع التكليف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I wish I had prepared for my life” means either doing useful good works now for the enduring afterlife or preparing for life after death.
rows.anchor: ليتني قدمت للحياة الباقية عملا صالحا ينفعني اليوم

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima interprets freeing a neck as freeing oneself from sins by repentance.
rows.anchor: فك رقبة قيل: فك [رقبته] من الذنوب بالتوبة، عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī reads freeing a neck as freeing oneself from punishment by taking on acts of obedience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد فك نفسه من العقاب بتحمل الطاعات، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: The majority of exegetes, including Abū ʿAlī and Abū Muslim, say it means emancipating male or female slaves.
rows.anchor: عن أكثر المفسرين، وهو قول أبي علي وأبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feeding is giving food during a day of hunger; an orphan is a child whose father died, while a person of kinship may be a relative.
rows.anchor: أو إطعام إعطاء الطعام في يوم ذي مسغبة أي: مجاعة يتيما الذي مات أبوه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid explain dhā matrabah as a poor person cast in the dirt with nothing to cover him from the ground.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس، ومجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Zayd derive matrabah from tariba, meaning a person became severely poor.
rows.anchor: شدة الحاجة من قولهم: ترب الرجل: إذا افتقر، عن ابن عباس، وابن زيد

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī describes someone so poor that he sticks to the dirt and owns nothing to shield his body from it.
rows.anchor: ذا متربة قد لصق بالتراب من الفقر، فليس له ما يقي نفسه من التراب

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim interprets the phrase as extreme poverty, using the Arabic expression for poverty that brings a person down to dust.
rows.anchor: أراد المفرط في الفقر، تقول العرب: فقر مدقع، أي: يلحق صاحبه بالدقعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma may mean “and,” so belief follows these acts; faith itself encompasses all acts of obedience.
rows.anchor: قيل: (ثم) بمعنى الواو؛ أي: وكان من الذين آمنوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mutual exhortation to patience means encouraging one another to obey and avoid disobedience; exhortation to compassion means mercy toward needy believers, relatives, and the oppressed.
rows.anchor: وصى بعضهم بعضا بالصبر على الطاعة وعن المعصية

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the people of the right receive their records in their right hands or are taken toward the right side.
rows.anchor: يأخذون كتبهم بأيمانهم، وقيل: يؤخذ بهم ناحية اليمين، كلا الوجهين ذكره أبو علي

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Abū Muslim gloss the people of the right as people of good fortune and blessing.
rows.anchor: أصحاب اليمن والبركة، عن الحسن، وأبي مسلم

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the people of the left receive their records in their left hands or are taken toward the left.
rows.anchor: يأخذون كتبهم بشمالهم، ويؤخذ بهم ذات الشمال، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim interprets the people of the left as people of ill fortune.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أهل الشؤم، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say muʾṣadah means covered over or shut.
rows.anchor: مطبقة، عن ابن عباس، ومجاهد، والضحاك

rows.speaker: أبي علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says its door is locked, to confirm that there is no hope of escape.
rows.anchor: مغلق بابها وهو الوصيد، وذلك لتأكيد اليأس من الروح، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to cross the obstacle urges struggle against the self through obedience, avoidance of sins, and suppression of desire; the following verses specify how to cross it.
rows.anchor: على الحث على مجاهدة النفس في عمل الطاعة، واجتناب المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw in this sūra’s openings is the oath particle and puts following nouns in genitive; the oath particles are bāʾ, then its derivative wāw, then tāʾ, which only precedes God’s name.
rows.anchor: الواو في قوله: (والشمس) ونظائرها واو القسم ولذلك كسر ما بعدها

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says an implicit lām belongs with qad aflaḥ, yielding la-qad aflaḥa.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل: اللام مضمر فيه، أي: لقد أفلح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another grammatical account has fronting and postponement, estimating “successful is the one who purifies it,” ahead of the sun oath.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل فيه تقديم وتأخير، تقديره: قد أفلح من زكاها والشمس وضحاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in jallāhā may return to the sun—its light reveals its disk—or to an understood darkness, as in descriptions such as a morning becoming cold without naming what is cold.
rows.anchor: والضمير في (جلاها) قيل: يعود على الشمس، وقد تقدم ذكرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sun is sworn by for its signs and blessings, or the ellipsis means “by the Lord of the sun.”
rows.anchor: واختلفوا، فقيل: القسم بالشمس لما فيه من الدلالة والنعمة

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid gloss the sun’s ḍuḥā as its light.
rows.anchor: قيل: ضوؤها، عن الحسن، ومجاهد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes the sun’s ḍuḥā as the whole day.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النهار كله، عن قتادة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil interprets ḍuḥā as the sun’s heat and links it to the Qur’anic description of being neither thirsty nor exposed to sunlight.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حرها، كقوله: (وأنك لا تظمأ فيها ولا تضحى) عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim says ḍuḥā describes the sun’s height and course from its morning ascent to its decline after noon; another gloss is sunrise and brightness.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طولها وارتفاعها في الضحى أي: أول النهار، وأفولها وانحطاطها بعد الزوال

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the moon follows the sun in light, in rising and setting, or across the two halves of the month; the crescent-night gloss is attributed to al-Ḥasan.
rows.anchor: والقمر إذا تلاها أي: تبعها، يعني: تبع الشمس

rows.speaker: أبي علي وأبي مسلم
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī and Abū Muslim gloss the moon following the sun as rising after it.
rows.anchor: والقمر إذا تلاها أي: تبعها، يعني: تبع الشمس

rows.speaker: أبي علي وأبي مسلم وجماعة
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī, Abū Muslim, and others say daytime reveals and illuminates the sun, because daylight comes from illumination and the sun.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النهار إذا جلى الشمس، وأنارها، وكشفها بإضاءتها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and others make the implicit object of “reveals” the darkness, which sunrise removes so everything becomes visible.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النهار إذا جلى الشمس، وأنارها، وكشفها بإضاءتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night covers and hides the sun at sunset and darkens the horizons; the pronoun cannot refer to day, since nahār is grammatically masculine.
rows.anchor: والليل إذا يغشاها أي: يغطي الشمس حين الغروب فيسترها

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda treats mā as a verbal noun: by the sky’s construction—its creation, elevation, arrangement, and adornment with stars.
rows.anchor: وما: المصدر، أي: وبنائها، يعني: بخلقها ورفعها وإسكانها وتزيينها بالكواكب

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid instead take mā as “who,” meaning the one who built the sky; the cited Qur’anic usage supports this construction.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ومن بناها، عن الحسن، ومجاهد

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد وأبي علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Abū ʿAlī read mā as “who spread it,” with the earth spread out to be a dwelling for creation; Qatāda also allows “and its spreading.”
rows.anchor: والأرض وما طحاها أي: ومن بسطها، عن الحسن، ومجاهد، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: قتادة وأبي علي
rows.claim: Qatāda and Abū ʿAlī explain the shaping of the soul as proportioning its creation, limbs, senses, and channels.
rows.anchor: ونفس وما سواها أي: تسويتها بأن عدل خلقها وأعضاءها وحواسها ومجاريها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan supplies “God” as the maker: God built the sky, spread the earth, and fashioned the soul.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ونفس وما سواها الله، والسماء وما بناها الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another construction takes the oath to be by the sky and its builder, the earth and its spreader, and the soul and its shaper.
rows.anchor: أقسم بالسماء ومن بناها، والأرض ومن دحاها، والنفس ومن سواها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة وسفيان والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, Sufyān, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say God inspired the soul by clarifying and teaching it wickedness and reverence.
rows.anchor: أي: بين لها الخير والشر، وعرفها الفجور والتقوى، عن ابن عباس، ومجاهد

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abū Muslim connects the fāʾ of “inspired it” to “the soul and what shaped it,” meaning God shaped the soul and then inspired it.
rows.anchor: والفاء في قوله: فألهمها عطف على قوله: (ونفس وما سواها)
